title: Nitro College
subtitle: Turning scattered screens into an end-to-end platform — by delivering a system, not just pages

meta.value: Product Owner · Project Manager · User Researchers · Consultants · Engineers

meta.value: Consumer web platform — college financial planning

indexedSections.title: A box of puzzle pieces, not a picture

value: As college costs and student-loan debt keep rising, planning for college has become overwhelming for families. Sallie Mae's Nitro College set out to improve financial readiness by guiding users through planning with clear action steps and timely reminders. I joined as the solo designer, owning execution end-to-end and defining the platform's foundational design.

What I inherited wasn't a product — it was a set of scattered puzzle pieces. The early designs were isolated screens: each looked fine alone, but they didn't add up to a journey. Moving from Dashboard to Profile to Scholarships, the experience broke apart. And underneath, there was no foundation at all: no design system, no button or input states, and none of the error and empty states real users hit every day.
As the only designer, I knew polishing screens one by one would only produce nicer puzzle pieces.

blocks.label: The delivery goal
blocks.value: Not to ship pages — to ship one end-to-end journey on a foundation that could keep scaling.

blocks.label: The end-to-end journey the scattered screens had to add up to

indexedSections.title: Four decisions that turned pieces into a product

blocks.title: Build the foundation before the surface

value: I made a counter-intuitive call: with business screens under pressure, I paused to build the design system first. The logic was simple — as one person guarding consistency across dozens of screens, manual pixel-matching would inevitably drift. I needed the system to hold consistency, not my own discipline.

I consolidated scattered brand assets into a single style guide, defined base components — buttons, inputs — with all their states, and abstracted reusable patterns: College Bridge, Nitro Outlook Tooltip, Offers.

The hard part was calibrating the level of abstraction — too abstract and a pattern is unusable; too shallow and it only fits one page. My rule: a pattern had to serve at least three real scenarios elegantly, or I'd abstracted at the wrong level. Once the foundation existed, every new page became assembly — faster, and consistent by construction.

blocks.label: The math I sold the team
blocks.value: Two extra weeks on the system up front doubled delivery speed and consistency on every page after. Solo, there is no other sustainable way.

blocks.label: The style guide — colors, typography, full UI palette, and buttons in every state

blocks.title: Treat the least glamorous work as the quality bar

value: Next I did what many skip: systematically completing every edge case. The original designs only drew the "happy path." But real users live in the unhappy paths — no data yet, a failed load, zero scholarship matches. The old screens dropped straight into blank pages.
So I ran every page through the three fates of data:

items.label: Fate 1
items.title: Has data
items.desc: The happy path — the only state the original designs drew.

items.label: Fate 2
items.title: No data
items.desc: An empty state with guidance: what this is, and what to do next.

items.label: Fate 3
items.title: Bad data
items.desc: An error state that speaks plain language instead of dead-ending.

blocks.value: A product's reliability lives not in its prettiest screen, but in its most awkward one. For an anxious parent using a financial product, those boundary moments are exactly where trust is won or lost.

blocks.title: One adaptive system for two different users

value: There was a structural tension: the platform serves two primary users — parents and students — with different goals, financial literacy, and priorities. Rather than build two separate interfaces (unmaintainable for one designer), I made one system adapt.

items.title: Adaptive Dashboard
items.desc: Content adjusts to the user's selected college — so the layout had to hold many data shapes gracefully: data-rich, data-sparse, and data-missing, not just one tidy sample.

items.title: Scholarships as a state system
items.desc: Liked / Applied / Won — a clear, predictable language that reads the same whether a parent or a student enters.

blocks.label: Two primary users — Alex, 17, high-school senior · Jean, 48, single mom of two

blocks.value: Commonality lives in one shared system; difference is handled by dynamic content — consistency and personalization solved at different layers.

value: Finally, scope. Nine months, solo — I couldn't build every feature. But an MVP's value isn't how much it does; it's whether it's a self-contained, complete loop.

I led a cross-functional feature-canvas workshop with product, engineering, and stakeholders to define each candidate feature's problem, value, and feasibility — turning ambiguity into decisive action. Then, working with the PM, I used Impact vs. Effort mapping to cut high-cost, low-value work and protect the core path: letting a user understand costs → find aid → plan funding, end to end.

I delivered a product that was deliberately scoped but experientially complete — not feature-full and half-finished. And because the foundation was a design system, post-MVP additions — shared parent/student account access, scholarship status tracking — could grow on top of it instead of forcing a rebuild.

indexedSections.title: Tested with real families, reviewed by real advisors

value: We validated the delivered experience on usertesting.com: 20-minute recorded sessions across up to 15 real tasks — 10 parents and guardians on desktop, 10 returning undergraduates on mobile — measured with SUS, NPS, CSAT, and mission-alignment surveys. We also ran one-hour moderated demo reviews with three Sallie Mae financial-aid advisors.

items.label: NPS
items.desc: Flagged as the area to improve

value: Most participants found the product intuitive and aligned with the mission of helping families plan with confidence, and the advisors gave a positive endorsement. NPS was honest feedback — and it directly shaped the post-MVP plan: an app tour, shared parent/student account access, and scholarship status tracking, all of which the design-system foundation could absorb without a rebuild.
I delivered not just a design version, but an extensible system and a complete journey.

indexedSections.title: Quality is set by the least glamorous details

value: Delivery quality isn't set by the brightest screen — it's set by the consistency of the system, the completeness of the edge cases, and the discipline of scope.

blocks.value: A high bar of execution and frictionless finance live precisely in the details others skip — and those details are where I'm most exacting.
